name: Acetaminophen
mechanism: Analgesic and antipyretic acting centrally. The FDA label states the precise mechanism is not established, only that it is thought to be primarily central — it is not an anti-inflammatory and does not affect platelets.
indications: Mild to moderate pain
Moderate to severe pain, alongside an opioid
Fever
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to acetaminophen
Severe hepatic impairment or severe active liver disease
pearls: No effect on platelet aggregation or small-vessel hemostasis — the label is explicit, which is why it is the analgesic of choice when bleeding is a concern
Overdose is hepatotoxic; the ceiling matters more than the single dose
Antipyretics lower a fever driven by the hypothalamus. They do not treat environmental hyperthermia — cool the patient

national.citation: NHTSA Scope of Practice Model 2019 (DOT HS 812 666), §V Medical Director Approved Medications, p. 36, AEMT column: "Oral over-the-counter (OTC) analgesics for pain or fever"

AEMT-C may give 500–1,000 mg IV as an alternative (optional stock)

name: Ibuprofen
mechanism: NSAID with analgesic and antipyretic activity. The label describes the mode of action as not completely understood, but probably prostaglandin synthetase (COX) inhibition.
indications: Mild to moderate pain
Fever
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to ibuprofen
Asthma, urticaria or allergic-type reaction after aspirin or another NSAID
In the setting of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery
pearls: The aspirin/NSAID cross-reaction is a contraindication in its own right, not a caution — severe and rarely fatal anaphylactoid reactions are reported
Prostaglandins hold the kidney’s afferent arterioles open; blocking them drops perfusion in chronic kidney disease and hypovolemia
RI layers further restrictions on top of the label — see the protocol detail below

riPearls: RI 2.07: 10 mg/kg PO (typical adult 400–800 mg), peds max 800 mg
RI: no NSAIDs in pregnancy, renal failure/transplant, active bleeding, suspected ICH, or possible surgery (open/deformed fractures)

name: Ketorolac
mechanism: NSAID with analgesic activity. The label describes the mechanism as not completely understood but probably prostaglandin synthetase inhibition, and notes it has no sedative or anxiolytic properties. Peak analgesic effect at 2–3 hours.
indications: Short-term (≤5 days) management of moderately severe acute pain requiring analgesia at the opioid level
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to ketorolac
Active peptic ulcer disease, recent GI bleeding or perforation — or any history of either
Asthma, urticaria or allergic-type reaction after aspirin or another NSAID
pearls: The label carries a Boxed Warning; the GI contraindication covers a past history, not just active bleeding, which is stricter than most NSAIDs
No sedation and no anxiolysis — an opioid-level analgesic that leaves the patient alert, which is its whole appeal
Prostaglandins hold the kidney’s afferent arterioles open; the same renal caution as ibuprofen applies

name: Aspirin
mechanism: The acetyl group binds a serine residue on COX-1, irreversibly inactivating the enzyme. Arachidonic acid can no longer become thromboxane A2, so the platelet cannot aggregate — for its whole 7–10 day lifespan.
indications: Chest pain suggestive of acute coronary syndrome
Reducing risk of death and MI in chronic coronary artery disease
Reducing risk of death and recurrent stroke after ischemic stroke or TIA
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to NSAIDs
The syndrome of asthma, rhinitis and nasal polyps — may cause severe urticaria, angioedema or bronchospasm
Active ulcer disease or active bleeding
Pediatric patients (Reye’s syndrome)
pearls: Irreversible is the point: the platelet has no nucleus and cannot make new COX-1, so effect lasts the platelet’s lifespan, not the drug’s half-life
The extended-release label carries a Limitation of Use — use immediate-release aspirin where rapid onset is needed, such as acute MI. Chewed, not swallowed whole
Aspirin-sensitive asthma travels with nasal polyps and rhinitis; ask about all three

national.citation: NHTSA Scope of Practice Model 2019 (DOT HS 812 666), §V Medical Director Approved Medications, p. 36, AEMT column: "Oral aspirin for chest pain of suspected ischemic origin"

name: Fentanyl citrate
mechanism: Opioid agonist. The label puts it plainly: its principal actions of therapeutic value are analgesia and sedation.
indications: Moderate to severe pain
Short-duration analgesia around anesthesia, and as an opioid analgesic supplement
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to fentanyl, including anaphylaxis
pearls: Hypersensitivity is the only contraindication the federal label lists — everything else in practice is a caution, dosed down rather than withheld
Little histamine release compared with morphine: less hypotension and less bronchospasm
Rapid IV push can cause chest wall rigidity and apnea — give it slowly

Repeat every 10 min to max 200 mcg adult, 150 mcg cumulative peds
Give IV over 2 minutes; reassess vitals before and 5 min after each dose

name: Albuterol
mechanism: Beta-adrenergic agonist. Stimulates adenyl cyclase, raising cyclic AMP inside the cell, which relaxes bronchial smooth muscle. Preferential for beta-2 receptors, the predominant receptor in bronchial smooth muscle.
indications: Relief of bronchospasm in reversible obstructive airway disease (asthma)
contraindications: History of hypersensitivity to any component
pearls: Beta-2 selectivity is preferential, not absolute — the label notes 10–50% of receptors in the human heart are beta-2, which is why tachycardia, tremor and chest tightness follow a dose
Tachydysrhythmia and severe coronary disease are cautions to weigh, not label contraindications
Routinely combined with ipratropium; RI authorises both at AEMT

national.citation: NHTSA Scope of Practice Model 2019 (DOT HS 812 666), §V Medical Director Approved Medications, p. 36, AEMT column: "Inhaled – beta agonist/bronchodilator and anticholinergic for dyspnea and wheezing"

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: ALBUTEROL SULFATE inhalation solution

riPearls: RI: 2.5–5 mg via SVN, ± ipratropium
AEMT-C: up to 3 doses in anaphylaxis

name: Terbutaline
mechanism: Beta-adrenergic agonist with a preferential effect on beta-2 receptors, relaxing bronchial smooth muscle. Given subcutaneously rather than inhaled, so it reaches a patient too tight to move air through a nebulizer.
indications: Prevention and reversal of bronchospasm in asthma, and reversible bronchospasm with bronchitis or emphysema, in patients 12 years and older
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to sympathomimetic amines or any component
Prolonged tocolysis beyond 48–72 hours, and maintenance tocolysis outpatient or at home — the subject of a Boxed Warning
pearls: The tocolysis Boxed Warning is the headline on this label and was missing from this card entirely
Subcutaneous, not inhaled — the reason to reach for it is a patient moving too little air for a nebulizer to work
Carried at no RI level, so it is here for recognition rather than for use

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: TERBUTALINE SULFATE injection, solution

riPearls: Not on the RI formulary. Reference only

name: Ipratropium bromide
mechanism: Anticholinergic (parasympatholytic). Antagonises acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, preventing the rise in intracellular calcium that would otherwise constrict the airway. It blocks vagally-mediated reflex bronchoconstriction rather than stimulating relaxation.
indications: Bronchospasm with COPD, including chronic bronchitis and emphysema (the labelled indication is maintenance)
Acute bronchospasm alongside a beta agonist — the prehospital use, authorised at AEMT by the national Scope of Practice Model and by RI
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to ipratropium bromide or any component
Hypersensitivity to atropine or any of its derivatives
pearls: Different lever from albuterol: albuterol pushes the muscle to relax, ipratropium stops the signal telling it to squeeze — which is why they are given together rather than one instead of the other
Minimal cardiac effect compared with a beta agonist; side effects are mostly local — dry mouth, cough
The atropine cross-sensitivity is a contraindication in its own right, worth asking about

national.citation: NHTSA Scope of Practice Model 2019 (DOT HS 812 666), §V Medical Director Approved Medications, p. 36, AEMT column: "Inhaled – beta agonist/bronchodilator and anticholinergic for dyspnea and wheezing"

name: Oxygen
mechanism: Raises the oxygen available to the blood so tissue can keep making ATP aerobically. It corrects hypoxemia; it does nothing for a patient whose problem is ventilation or perfusion rather than oxygen content.
indications: Hypoxemia from any cause — COPD, pneumonia, severe asthma, heart failure
Respiratory insufficiency
Carbon monoxide poisoning
pearls: Titrate to the patient rather than running high flow by reflex — oxygen corrects hypoxemia, and a patient who is already saturated gains nothing from more of it
Fire risk: no smoking, no flammable material near a patient on oxygen
Secure cylinders upright. A falling tank that loses its valve becomes a projectile
Nasal cannula 1–6 L/min; a nebulizer needs 6–8 L/min to aerosolize properly
Not listed in RI appendix 09.00 at all — it is carried as equipment at every level, not as a formulary medication

national.citation: NHTSA EMS Education Standards 2021 (amended 24 Feb 2025), Airway Management, Respiration and Ventilation, p. 35, AEMT column: "Supplemental oxygen therapy"

riPearls: RI 1.01: for possible cardiac etiology and/or SpO2 < 94%, titrate to the lowest concentration that maintains SpO2 94–99%

name: Lidocaine
mechanism: Class IB antiarrhythmic. In Purkinje fibers it attenuates phase 4 diastolic depolarization and decreases automaticity, shortening action potential duration and the effective refractory period. It suppresses the irritable tissue without much effect on healthy myocardium.
indications: Acute management of ventricular arrhythmias, such as those occurring with acute myocardial infarction or during cardiac manipulation
Prehospital protocol use (separate from cardiac SPL): Intraosseous (IO) analgesia prior to fluid infusion in conscious patients
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to amide-type local anesthetics
Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
Stokes-Adams syndrome
Severe sinoatrial, atrioventricular or intraventricular block without an artificial pacemaker
pearls: The WPW contraindication is on the federal label and was missing from this card entirely
Amide-type cross-sensitivity is the allergy question to ask — lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine all share it; the ester anesthetics do not
The IO-infusion-pain use is a different product label; this card is the cardiac arrhythmia label only

national.note: "Cardiac rhythms (C,C)" appears only in the Paramedic column (Standards p. 39).

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: LIDOCAINE HYDROCHLORIDE injection, solution (Hospira) — cardiac arrhythmia label

formulary.minimumQuantity: 1 gm/250 ml or 2 gm/500 ml (premixed) X X X

conflicts.nremt: AHA: 1–1.5 mg/kg, then 0.5–0.75 mg/kg, max 3 mg/kg
conflicts.ri: RI: flat 100 mg, repeat every 10 min × 2

riPearls: RI 3.03A: arrest 100 mg IV/IO, repeat every 10 min × 2 (alternative to or after amiodarone)
RI 3.07A: wide complex tachycardia 1–1.5 mg/kg
RI 3.03P: peds arrest 1 mg/kg (max 100 mg)

name: Procainamide
mechanism: Class IA antiarrhythmic. Lengthens the effective refractory period of the atria and, less so, the His-Purkinje system and ventricles, and slows conduction velocity. Its effect on the AV node is mixed — a direct slowing action set against a weaker vagolytic effect that can speed AV conduction.
indications: Documented, life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias such as sustained ventricular tachycardia
contraindications: Complete heart block — suppresses nodal and ventricular pacemakers, with a hazard of asystole
Known hypersensitivity to procainamide or procaine
pearls: Boxed Warning. The label restricts it to arrhythmias that are life-threatening in the physician’s judgement, explicitly because of proarrhythmic effects — the CAST trial showed excess mortality treating non-life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias
Complete heart block is hard to see behind a wide-complex tachycardia. If the rate slows during treatment with no AV conduction appearing, stop the drug
Long-term use is associated with a lupus-like syndrome and agranulocytosis — not a field concern, but it is why this drug fell out of favour

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: PROCAINAMIDE HYDROCHLORIDE injection

riPearls: RI: Paramedic only. Not in AEMT-C scope

name: Metoprolol
mechanism: Beta-1 selective (cardioselective) adrenergic blocker, slowing rate and AV conduction. The label is explicit that the selectivity is not absolute — at higher plasma concentrations it also blocks beta-2 receptors in bronchial and vascular smooth muscle. No intrinsic sympathomimetic activity.
indications: Definite or suspected acute myocardial infarction in hemodynamically stable patients, to reduce cardiovascular mortality
Prehospital / RI Paramedic protocol use (off-label on IV SPL): Rate control in atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter with rapid ventricular response
contraindications: Heart rate < 45 beats/min
Second- or third-degree heart block without a functioning pacemaker
Significant first-degree heart block — PR interval ≥ 0.24 sec
Systolic blood pressure < 100 mmHg
Decompensated cardiac failure
Hypersensitivity to metoprolol or to another beta blocker — cross-sensitivity occurs
pearls: The thresholds are numeric and testable: HR < 45, SBP < 100, PR ≥ 0.24 sec. The PR cutoff was missing from this card
Cardioselective is relative, not absolute — enough drug reaches beta-2 to matter in a patient with reactive airways
Rate control in AFib or SVT is a common off-label use; this IV label covers acute MI only

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: METOPROLOL TARTRATE injection

riPearls: RI: Paramedic only. Not in AEMT-C scope

name: Amiodarone
mechanism: Nominally a class III antiarrhythmic, but it carries electrophysiologic characteristics of all four Vaughan Williams classes — sodium channel block at rapid pacing frequencies, noncompetitive antisympathetic action, and prolongation of the cardiac action potential.
indications: Initiation and prophylaxis of frequently recurring ventricular fibrillation and hemodynamically unstable ventricular tachycardia, in patients refractory to other therapy
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to any component, including iodine
Cardiogenic shock
Marked sinus bradycardia
Second- or third-degree AV block without a functioning pacemaker
pearls: The iodine hypersensitivity is easy to miss and sits in the label’s contraindications — worth asking about shellfish and contrast reactions
All four Vaughan Williams classes in one molecule, which is why the side-effect profile reaches so far beyond rhythm
The label reserves it for arrhythmias refractory to other therapy, not as a first move

name: Diltiazem
mechanism: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. Inhibits calcium influx during depolarization in cardiac and vascular smooth muscle, slowing AV nodal conduction time and prolonging AV nodal refractoriness. Use-dependent — it works harder the faster the node is firing.
indications: Temporary control of rapid ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter
Rapid conversion of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia to sinus rhythm
contraindications: Atrial fibrillation or flutter with an accessory bypass tract, such as WPW syndrome
Ventricular tachycardia
Sick sinus syndrome, or second- or third-degree AV block without a functioning ventricular pacemaker
Severe hypotension or cardiogenic shock
Concomitant administration with IV beta-blockers
Demonstrated hypersensitivity to the drug
pearls: The two that kill: AFib with an accessory pathway, and any wide-complex tachycardia that might be VT. Blocking the AV node in pre-excited AFib pushes conduction down the bypass tract and can degenerate into VF
Both of those were absent from this card, which previously listed no contraindications at all
IV beta-blockers are a listed contraindication, not merely a caution — two AV nodal blockers together is the mechanism of the harm

national.note: As lidocaine.

conflicts.ri: RI: medical control first; max 20 mg, then max 25 mg only if SBP ≥100

riPearls: RI 3.06A: AEMT-C must contact MEDICAL CONTROL first
0.25 mg/kg IV, max 20 mg
If SBP ≥100, may repeat × 1 at 0.35 mg/kg, max 25 mg

name: Nitroglycerin
mechanism: Forms free radical nitric oxide, which activates guanylate cyclase and raises cyclic GMP in smooth muscle. Myosin light chains dephosphorylate and the vessel relaxes — venous capacitance first, dropping preload, so the ventricle has less to pump against and needs less oxygen.
indications: Acute relief of an attack of angina pectoris due to coronary artery disease
Acute prophylaxis of angina pectoris
contraindications: PDE-5 inhibitors — avanafil, sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil. Severe hypotension, syncope or myocardial ischemia can follow
Soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators such as riociguat
Severe anemia — large doses can oxidize hemoglobin to methemoglobin
Hypotension or hypovolemia
Right ventricular infarction, where the ventricle is preload-dependent
pearls: The card listed three PDE-5 drugs; the label names four and adds riociguat, a pulmonary hypertension drug that is easy to miss on a med list
Severe anemia is a label contraindication via methemoglobin, and was absent here
This is the sublingual label — the formulation RI carries at EMT (patient’s own supply), AEMT and AEMT-C. Infusion and transdermal are different labels and different scope

Avoid in right ventricular infarction (preload dependent)
Under 16 yo without known coronary disease: medical control first

name: Furosemide
mechanism: Loop diuretic. Inhibits reabsorption of sodium and chloride in the proximal and distal tubules and the loop of Henle, producing rapid diuresis. The venodilatory effect arrives before the diuresis does.
indications: Edema associated with congestive heart failure, where oral therapy is not feasible or the situation is an emergency
contraindications: Anuria
History of hypersensitivity to furosemide
pearls: The label’s contraindications are only anuria and hypersensitivity. Hypovolemia, hypotension and hypokalemia are cautions that were sitting in the contraindications field
Parenteral therapy is reserved for patients who cannot take oral or who are in an emergency — the label says so directly
Cirrhotic and chronic renal edema are on the label but are not prehospital presentations, so they are left off this card

national.note: Pulmonary edema is an AEMT condition (Standards p. 44); the drug is not nationally authorised.

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: FUROSEMIDE injection

riPearls: RI 3.01: second-tier only
Only if transport ≥30 min, patient already takes oral furosemide, and SBP ≥100
Give the patient's usual daily dose IV, max 80 mg

name: Diazepam
mechanism: Benzodiazepine acting on the limbic system, thalamus and hypothalamus to produce calming. Unlike the phenothiazines it has no peripheral autonomic blocking action and produces no extrapyramidal effects.
indications: Adjunct in status epilepticus
Acute alcohol withdrawal — agitation, tremor, impending or acute delirium tremens
Skeletal muscle spasm from local pathology, trauma or spasticity
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to diazepam
Acute narrow-angle glaucoma
Open-angle glaucoma, unless the patient is on appropriate therapy
pearls: Labelled for status epilepticus as an adjunct — unlike midazolam, where the seizure use is off-label
The glaucoma contraindication splits: narrow-angle is absolute, open-angle is permitted if treated
RI stocks it as the optional interchangeable alternative to lorazepam (appendix 09.01), so your service carries one or the other

national.note: As midazolam.

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: DIAZEPAM injection, solution

riPearls: RI carries diazepam OR lorazepam (interchangeable; service picks)
RI 2.19A: 2.5 mg IV/IN every 5 min, max 10 mg
RI 2.19P: 0.1 mg/kg IN/IV (max 2.5 mg per dose) or 0.5 mg/kg PR (max 20 mg per dose); total max 10 mg
Longest half-life: least desirable benzo when others are available; no IM in peds

name: Lorazepam
mechanism: Binds the GABA-benzodiazepine receptor complex with relatively high and specific affinity, which the label presumes to be the basis of its action — enhancing GABA-mediated inhibition throughout the brain.
indications: Status epilepticus
contraindications: Known sensitivity to benzodiazepines
Sensitivity to the vehicle — polyethylene glycol, propylene glycol or benzyl alcohol
Acute narrow-angle glaucoma
Sleep apnea syndrome
Severe respiratory insufficiency, except where the patient is mechanically ventilated
Intra-arterial administration
pearls: The vehicle is a contraindication in its own right — polyethylene glycol, propylene glycol and benzyl alcohol, which matters for neonates and small children
Intra-arterial administration is contraindicated outright; the vehicle can cause arterial spasm and gangrene
Sleep apnea and severe respiratory insufficiency are listed contraindications, not cautions — the narrowest respiratory profile of the three benzodiazepines on this list

RI 2.19A: 2 mg IV/IM every 5 min, max 10 mg
RI 2.19P: 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 2 mg per dose), total max 10 mg
Heat-sensitive: expires in 6 weeks unrefrigerated

name: Midazolam
mechanism: Short-acting benzodiazepine CNS depressant. Water-soluble in the vial and lipophilic at physiologic pH, which is why it crosses into the CNS quickly and wears off quickly.
indications: Sedation, anxiolysis and amnesia before or during a procedure
Continuous infusion for sedation of intubated and mechanically ventilated patients
Prehospital / RI protocol use (off-label on this SPL): seizure termination and acute agitation
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to midazolam
Acute narrow-angle glaucoma
Open-angle glaucoma only if the patient is on appropriate therapy
pearls: Seizure use is NOT on this label — diazepam and lorazepam are labelled for status epilepticus, midazolam is not, even though RI carries it as Required at AEMT-C
Boxed Warning: respiratory depression and respiratory arrest. The label was written around a monitored setting with resuscitation immediately available
Risk compounds with opioids — the combination is the subject of a class-wide Boxed Warning

national.note: Seizure is an AEMT condition (Standards p. 42); benzodiazepines appear in no national medication row.

conflicts.ri: RI: 0.1 mg/kg, max 2 mg per dose

RI 2.19P: 0.1 mg/kg IV/IM/IN (max 2 mg per dose), cumulative max 1 mg/kg
RI 2.25: agitated delirium 2.5–5 mg IV or 5 mg IM/IN, repeat in 10 min if SBP >100, max 10 mg

name: Activated charcoal
mechanism: A porous carbon matrix that adsorbs poison in the stomach, reducing absorption. It also works long after ingestion by interrupting enterohepatic and enterovascular recirculation of the poison (NLM PubChem, CID 5462310).
indications: Emergency use to adsorb swallowed poisons
contraindications: Persons who are not fully conscious
After ingestion of corrosives — alkalies such as lye, or strong acids — unless directed by a health professional
After ingestion of petroleum distillates such as kerosene, gasoline, paint thinner, cleaning fluid or furniture polish, or turpentine, unless directed by a health professional
pearls: The label’s own wording is "do not use in persons who are not fully conscious" — the risk is aspiration of a charcoal slurry into an unprotected airway

It does not adsorb everything. General toxicology, not from this label: pesticides and petroleum, heavy metals including iron and lithium, acids and alkalis, alcohols, and solvents including cyanide pass straight through
The label also says not to give it until after the patient has vomited, unless a health professional directs otherwise
Carried at no RI level and absent from the RI protocols entirely — this card is for recognition, not for use

national.note: Absent from §V; largely withdrawn from practice.

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: ACTIDOSE AQUA (activated charcoal) suspension — OTC Drug Facts label

riPearls: Not on the RI formulary. Reference only

name: Hydroxocobalamin
mechanism: Cyanide binds cytochrome a3 and arrests cellular respiration, which is why a high dose kills within minutes. Hydroxocobalamin binds the cyanide ion to form cyanocobalamin — vitamin B12 — which the kidney excretes.
indications: Known or suspected cyanide poisoning
pearls: The label lists NO contraindications — in suspected cyanide poisoning there is nothing to weigh it against
Deep red colour causes transient chromaturia and erythema in over 5% of patients. The skin stays discoloured, and the label advises avoiding direct sun while it does, for photosensitivity
Label §5.5: the red colour interferes with colorimetric lab determinations — clinical chemistry, hematology, coagulation and urine parameters. Warn the receiving facility
Label §5.7: a blood cyanide level is not required to treat and must not delay treatment, though a pretreatment sample is useful for documentation
Serious reactions are allergic reactions, renal injury and raised blood pressure; monitor pressure during infusion

national.note: Cyanide antidote; federal guidance in CHEMM, but not a national AEMT medication.

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: CYANOKIT (hydroxocobalamin) injection, powder, lyophilized

riPearls: RI 4.18/4.20: if available, 70 mg/kg IV (max 5 g) in 250 mL NS over 15 min; faster in arrest

name: Atropine + pralidoxime
mechanism: Two drugs, two receptor families. Atropine competitively blocks excess acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors — smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, secretory glands, autonomic ganglia and CNS. Pralidoxime reactivates the acetylcholinesterase the organophosphate has inhibited, which is what restores function at the nicotinic sites atropine cannot reach.
indications: Poisoning by organophosphorus nerve agents and organophosphorus insecticides, in adults and pediatric patients over 41 kg (90 lb)
pearls: The label lists NO contraindications. Against a life-threatening nerve agent exposure there is nothing on the other side of the scale
Atropine handles the muscarinic signs — the wet ones. Pralidoxime is what reaches the nicotinic signs, the fasciculations and weakness, by freeing the enzyme itself
Pralidoxime works best before the inhibited enzyme ages; delay costs effect, which is the argument for the auto-injector
Weight floor of 41 kg (90 lb) is on the label, so this kit is not a pediatric solution
Appendix 09.01 lists DuoDote and the Mark-1 NAAK as interchangeable, and the national Scope of Practice Model marks auto-injector antidotes at every level including EMR

national.note: Marked at every level, EMR through Paramedic.

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: DUODOTE (atropine and pralidoxime chloride) kit; federal guidance at ASPR CHEMM (chemm.hhs.gov)

name: Naloxone
mechanism: Opioid antagonist that prevents or reverses the effects of opioids — respiratory depression, sedation and hypotension. It also reverses the psychotomimetic and dysphoric effects of agonist-antagonists such as pentazocine.
indications: Complete or partial reversal of opioid depression, including respiratory depression, from natural and synthetic opioids
Reversal of mixed agonist-antagonists — nalbuphine, pentazocine, butorphanol, cyclazocine
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to naloxone or any ingredient
pearls: Hypersensitivity is the only contraindication on the label — the real constraint is the dose, not whether to give it
Titrate to respiration, not to consciousness. Abrupt complete reversal in an opioid-dependent patient precipitates acute withdrawal
The antagonist can outlast or be outlasted by the opioid; a patient who wakes can go back down, which is why transport still matters

national.citation: NHTSA Scope of Practice Model 2019 (DOT HS 812 666), §V Medical Director Approved Medications, p. 36, AEMT column: "Use of opioid antagonist auto-injector for suspected opioid overdose"
national.note: Also "Intranasal - opioid antagonist for suspected opioid overdose", same table.

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: NALOXONE HYDROCHLORIDE injection

riPearls: RI 4.18A: 0.4–4 mg IN or 0.4 mg IV/IM every 3–5 min to adequate ventilation, max 10 mg
RI 4.18P: <20 kg → 0.1 mg/kg (max 2 mg); ≥20 kg → 2 mg IN
Ventilate with a BVM first

name: Dextrose
mechanism: Restores blood glucose and supplies carbohydrate calories, giving the cell substrate for ATP production.
indications: Insulin-induced hypoglycemia, including hyperinsulinemia and insulin shock
contraindications: Intracranial or intraspinal hemorrhage — concentrated dextrose can worsen cerebral edema by shifting fluid across the blood-brain barrier
Severe dehydration — risk of worsening a hyperosmolar state
Alcohol withdrawal — can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy or cardiomyopathy in a thiamine-deficient patient
Known hypersensitivity to dextrose
pearls: The Wernicke contraindication is why thiamine goes first in a patient with alcohol use or malnutrition — it is on the federal label, not just protocol folklore
Concentrated dextrose is sclerosing: extravasation causes tissue damage, so confirm the line before pushing
This is the 50% label. RI carries D10 at AEMT and AEMT-C and D5 at Paramedic only — the contraindications are properties of concentrated dextrose and carry across

national.citation: NHTSA EMS Education Standards 2021 (amended 24 Feb 2025), Medicine / Endocrine Disorders, p. 40, AEMT column: "Diabetic emergencies (C,F)"
national.note: IV route approved at AEMT in the Model’s §V "Intravenous" row.

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: DEXTROSE (dextrose monohydrate) injection, solution — 50% label

formulary.minimumQuantity: One (1) 250 ml bag, One (1) 500 ml X X X

conflicts.nremt: Textbook: D50 25 g adult; D10 also taught
conflicts.ri: RI: D10 only; adult 250 mL (25 g), peds 5 mL/kg

riPearls: RI carries D10 only (no D50)
Treat when bG ≤60 mg/dL and patient can't take oral glucose
RI 2.10A: D10 250 mL (25 g) IV over 5 min, repeat in 5 min if bG <60
RI 2.10P: D10 5 mL/kg over 5 min, repeat if bG <60
Thiamine 200 mg first if alcohol use or malnourished

name: Glucagon
mechanism: Raises blood glucose by acting on liver glycogen, converting it to glucose. The label is specific that it acts ONLY on liver glycogen. Parenterally it also relaxes smooth muscle of the stomach, duodenum, small bowel and colon.
indications: Severe hypoglycemia in patients with diabetes mellitus
Prehospital / RI protocol use (off-label on the hypoglycemia SPL): Beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker toxicity and beta-blocked refractory anaphylaxis
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to glucagon
Known pheochromocytoma — glucagon can provoke catecholamine release
pearls: It only works if there is liver glycogen to mobilize. In starvation, adrenal insufficiency or chronic hypoglycemia the stores are already empty and glucagon will not raise the sugar
Caution with insulinoma: the label warns an initial glucose rise can make the tumour release insulin, dropping the patient into rebound hypoglycemia
Type 1 patients get less of a glucose rise than stable type 2 patients — the label says so, and supplementary carbohydrate matters once they can swallow

national.citation: NHTSA EMS Education Standards 2021 (amended 24 Feb 2025), Medicine / Endocrine Disorders, p. 40, AEMT column: "Diabetic emergencies (C,F)"

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: GLUCAGON kit (glucagon for injection)

riPearls: RI 2.10A: 1 mg IM or 3 mg IN (Baqsimi) if no IV
RI 2.10P: 0.1 mg/kg IM, max 1 mg
RI 2.04A: 1–4 mg IV in anaphylaxis on a beta blocker

name: Sodium bicarbonate
mechanism: Dissociates to sodium and bicarbonate. The bicarbonate buffers excess hydrogen ion, raises plasma bicarbonate and blood pH, and reverses the clinical manifestations of acidosis.
indications: Metabolic acidosis — including cardiac arrest, circulatory insufficiency from shock or severe dehydration, severe renal disease, uncontrolled diabetes and severe primary lactic acidosis
Hyperkalemia
Alkalinization in drug toxicity — tricyclic antidepressant and sodium-channel-blocker overdose
contraindications: Patients losing chloride through vomiting or continuous gastrointestinal suction
Patients on diuretics known to produce a hypochloremic alkalosis
Alkalosis
Hypocalcemia, where alkalosis can precipitate tetany
pearls: Sodium load matters: the label warns to use it with great care, if at all, in congestive heart failure, severe renal insufficiency, or edema with sodium retention
Raising pH drives potassium back into cells — the reason it works in hyperkalemia, and the reason it can unmask hypocalcemic tetany
Incompatible with calcium chloride: flush the line between them or they precipitate

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: SODIUM BICARBONATE injection, USP

riPearls: Incompatible with calcium chloride: flush between
RI 2.25: 50 mEq IV if agitated-delirium patient arrests

riAuthority.note: Medical Control required at AEMT-C for toxicology (4.18), crush injury and hyperkalemia (4.09), and the dialysis protocol. Standing order in cardiac arrest per 2.25. At Paramedic level the same orders read "consider", with no contact required.

name: Hydrocortisone / methylprednisolone
mechanism: Synthetic glucocorticoid. Potent anti-inflammatory that also modifies the body’s immune response, damping the inflammatory cascade and the capillary leak behind it.
indications: Severe or incapacitating allergic conditions, when oral therapy is not feasible
Asthma or COPD exacerbation
Adrenal insufficiency (hydrocortisone)
contraindications: Systemic fungal infections
Known hypersensitivity to the product or its constituents
The 40 mg methylprednisolone presentation contains lactose from cow’s milk — contraindicated with known or suspected milk hypersensitivity
pearls: Onset is 1–2 hours. It is never a substitute for epinephrine in anaphylaxis — give epinephrine first and treat this as the follow-on
RI appendix 09.00 codes three agents separately: dexamethasone is Choice at AEMT-C while hydrocortisone and methylprednisolone are Required, so what your service stocks varies
The cow’s-milk contraindication is presentation-specific, not drug-wide — worth knowing which vial you carry

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: METHYLPREDNISOLONE SODIUM SUCCINATE injection, powder, for solution

riPearls: RI 2.04A: methylprednisolone 125 mg IV or hydrocortisone 100 mg IV
RI 2.04P: 2 mg/kg IV (methylpred max 60 mg, hydrocortisone max 100 mg)
Onset 1–2 hr: never a substitute for epinephrine

name: Oxymetazoline
mechanism: Adrenergic alpha-agonist (NLM RxClass, MED-RT mechanism of action). Alpha-1 stimulation constricts the nasal mucosal vessels, shrinking swollen membranes and slowing bleeding from them.
indications: Epistaxis (RI protocol use — not an FDA-labelled indication)
Temporary relief of nasal and sinus congestion (the labelled indication)
contraindications: No contraindications section exists on the OTC label — treat known hypersensitivity as the practical limit
pearls: The OTC Drug Facts label has no Clinical Pharmacology or Contraindications section, so mechanism here is cited to RxClass rather than to a federal label that does not contain it
Epistaxis is the RI indication; the label itself only claims decongestion. Vasoconstriction is the same action either way
Rebound congestion follows repeated use — a discharge concern, not a field one

national.note: Epistaxis is an AEMT condition (Standards p. 39), but §V marks the topical route Paramedic-only.

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: NASAL (oxymetazoline hydrochloride) spray — OTC label (indications); mechanism from NLM RxClass MED-RT has_MoA

name: Epinephrine
mechanism: Acts on both alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptors. Alpha-1 vasoconstriction raises pressure and reverses mucosal edema; beta-1 raises rate and contractility; beta-2 relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and stabilises mast cells.
indications: Anaphylaxis
Cardiac arrest
pearls: The label lists NO contraindications. In anaphylaxis there is nothing to weigh against it — delay is the danger, not the drug
1:1,000 is the IM concentration; 1:10,000 is the IV/arrest concentration. RI codes them as separate formulary rows, and mixing them up is the classic drug error
Nebulised 2.25% racemic epinephrine for croup is a third preparation entirely, carried only at AEMT-C in RI

formulary.minimumQuantity: 3 mg (auto-injector/prefilled syringe/ R R R R

conflicts.nremt: AHA: 1 mg every 3–5 min, no set max
conflicts.ri: RI: every 5 min, max 5 doses (non-shockable) or 3 (shockable)

conflicts.nremt: AHA 2025: 0.01 mg/kg, max 1 mg, every 3–5 min

riPearls: RI 2.04A: 0.3 mg IM (1 mg/mL) lateral thigh, every 5 min, max 3 doses
Over 50 yo or cardiac history: 0.15 mg
RI 2.04P: 0.15 mg for 15–30 kg, 0.3 mg for >30 kg
RI 3.03A: arrest 1 mg (1 mg/10 mL) IV/IO every 5 min; max 5 doses non-shockable, 3 doses shockable
AEMT (A level) gives IV epi only for non-shockable arrest
RI 3.03P: peds arrest 0.01 mg/kg of 1 mg/10 mL

name: Adenosine
mechanism: Slows conduction through the AV node and can interrupt re-entry pathways running through it, restoring sinus rhythm in paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia.
indications: Regular narrow complex tachycardia (SVT)
Regular monomorphic wide complex tachycardia
contraindications: Second- or third-degree AV block, except with a functioning artificial pacemaker
Sinus node disease — sick sinus syndrome or symptomatic bradycardia — except with a functioning artificial pacemaker
Known hypersensitivity to adenosine
pearls: The label says to AVOID it in bronchoconstriction or bronchospasm such as asthma, where it can cause bronchoconstriction through mast cell degranulation. That sits in Warnings rather than Contraindications, but it is the asthma question you ask before pushing

New rhythm disturbances at the moment of conversion occur in 55% of patients — PACs, PVCs, brief AFib, sinus bradycardia, varying AV block. Transient asystole and, rarely, VF have been reported, including fatal cases
The half-life is seconds, which is why it goes in as a rapid push followed immediately by a flush, and why the alarming pause self-resolves

national.note: As lidocaine.

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: ADENOSINE injection, solution

conflicts.nremt: AHA: 6 mg rapid IVP, then 12 mg
AHA 2025: 0.1 mg/kg (max 6 mg), then 0.2 mg/kg (max 12 mg)
conflicts.ri: RI 3.06P: 0.2 mg/kg (max 12 mg) first, with medical control

riPearls: RI 3.06A: 12 mg rapid IV push, may repeat × 1
RI 3.07A notes: some patients start at a reduced 6 mg
RI 3.06P: 0.2 mg/kg (max 12 mg) with MEDICAL CONTROL at AEMT-C

name: Atropine sulfate
mechanism: Competitively blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors — smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, secretory glands, peripheral autonomic ganglia and the CNS. Removing vagal tone from the SA and AV nodes speeds the rate.
indications: Symptomatic bradycardia
pearls: The federal label lists NO contraindications. The limits on atropine are limits of EFFECT, not of safety, which is a distinction worth holding

It works at the AV node and above. In infranodal block — Mobitz II, or third-degree block with a wide QRS — the escape focus is below the node and atropine has nothing to act on. Pace rather than waiting on a second dose
A transplanted heart is denervated, so there is no vagal tone to block and atropine does nothing
Same molecule as the atropine half of DuoDote, used against a different problem: there, excess acetylcholine from organophosphate poisoning

national.note: As lidocaine. Distinct from the DuoDote auto-injector row.

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: ATROPINE SULFATE injection, USP

conflicts.nremt: AHA: 1 mg every 3–5 min, max 3 mg
conflicts.ri: RI: 0.5–1 mg every 3–5 min, max 3 mg

riPearls: RI 3.05A: 0.5–1 mg IV every 3–5 min to HR >60, max 3 mg
RI 3.05P: 0.02 mg/kg, min 0.1 mg, max single dose 0.5 mg, may repeat × 1

name: Ondansetron
mechanism: Selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonist. The label notes the mechanism is not fully characterised and is explicit that it is NOT a dopamine-receptor antagonist.
indications: Nausea / vomiting
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity, including anaphylaxis, to ondansetron or any component
Concomitant apomorphine — profound hypotension and loss of consciousness have been reported
pearls: Apomorphine is a true contraindication on the label, not an interaction caution — profound hypotension and loss of consciousness
Not a dopamine antagonist, so it does not carry the extrapyramidal side effects of the older antiemetics
Dose-dependent QT prolongation is the reason the 32 mg single IV dose was withdrawn; keep it in mind in a patient already prolonged

national.note: No antiemetic row in the Model’s §V; paramedic-level by convention.

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: ONDANSETRON HYDROCHLORIDE injection

conflicts.ri: RI: weight bands, 2 mg (10–20 kg) or 4 mg (>20 kg)

riPearls: RI 2.07A: 4 mg PO/SL/IV/IM/ODT, may repeat × 1 in 15 min
RI 2.07P: only >3 months and >10 kg; 10–20 kg → 2 mg, >20 kg → 4 mg (weight bands, not mg/kg)

name: Diphenhydramine
mechanism: Antihistamine that competes with histamine for receptor sites on effector cells, with anticholinergic (drying) and sedative effects of its own.
indications: Allergic reaction / anaphylaxis (adjunct)
contraindications: Neonates and premature infants
Nursing mothers
Use as a local anesthetic
pearls: It competes with histamine rather than displacing it — which is why it cannot undo the histamine already bound, and why it is an adjunct to epinephrine in anaphylaxis, never a substitute
The neonate and premature-infant contraindication is absolute on the label, and extends to nursing mothers
The anticholinergic load is the side-effect profile: dry mouth, urinary retention, sedation, and delirium in the elderly

national.note: Anaphylaxis is an AEMT condition (Standards p. 41) but §V authorises only the epinephrine auto-injector.

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: DIPHENHYDRAMINE HYDROCHLORIDE injection

riPearls: RI 2.04A: 50 mg PO/IV/IM
RI 2.04P: 1 mg/kg (max 50 mg)
Over 65 yo: consider cetirizine 10 mg PO instead
Treats rash and itch only: never replaces epinephrine

name: Thiamine (vitamin B1)
mechanism: Water-soluble vitamin B1. The body cannot store it long, and without it the enzymes of aerobic glucose metabolism stall — which is why a thiamine-deficient patient given glucose can decompensate.
indications: Hypoglycemia in patients with alcohol use or malnutrition
contraindications: History of sensitivity to thiamine or any ingredient
pearls: The partner drug to dextrose: the 50% dextrose label contraindicates use in alcohol withdrawal precisely because glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy
Labelled for thiamine deficiency and beriberi, dry (nervous system) or wet (cardiovascular)
Sensitivity is the only contraindication on the label; the WARNINGS section is where the rare anaphylactoid reaction to IV administration sits

national.note: Alcohol withdrawal is an AEMT condition (Standards p. 44); the drug appears in no national source.

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: THIAMINE HYDROCHLORIDE injection, solution

riPearls: RI 2.10A: 200 mg IV/IM before D10
Optional at AEMT, required stock at AEMT-C

name: Calcium chloride 10%
mechanism: Supplies ionic calcium, essential to the functional integrity of nerve and muscle and to myocardial contractility. In hyperkalemia it does not lower potassium — it raises the threshold potential back away from the resting potential, stabilising the membrane.
indications: Hypocalcemia, including hydrofluoric acid burns
Hyperkalemia — to stabilise the myocardium
Calcium channel blocker or beta blocker toxicity
contraindications: Cardiac resuscitation in the presence of ventricular fibrillation
Patients at risk of existing digitalis toxicity
Not recommended in asystole or electromechanical dissociation
pearls: The VF contraindication is specific and easy to miss: contraindicated for cardiac resuscitation while VF is present
Digitalis toxicity is the other hard stop — calcium worsens digoxin-induced arrhythmia
Sclerosing. Extravasation causes tissue necrosis and sloughing, so confirm the line and flush between this and sodium bicarbonate, which it precipitates with
Interchangeable with calcium gluconate per RI appendix 09.01; the gluconate is gentler on a peripheral vein

source.doc: DailyMed SPL: CALCIUM CHLORIDE injection, 10%

riPearls: RI 4.08: 1 g slow IV, may repeat × 1
Interchangeable with calcium gluconate (service picks)
Incompatible with sodium bicarbonate

riAuthority.note: Medical Control required at AEMT-C everywhere it is given in v2026.02: beta-blocker/CCB toxicity (4.18), crush injury and hyperkalemia (4.09), and the dialysis protocol. At Paramedic level the same orders read "consider", with no contact required.

name: Nitrous oxide 50/50
mechanism: RI 7.41 states the exact mechanism is unknown. Its effects occur in the pain centres of the brain and spinal cord, thought to involve release of endogenous opioid peptides and serotonin activating descending inhibitory pathways, plus a GABA effect producing drowsiness. Onset 30–60 seconds, peak at 2–5 minutes.
indications: Moderate to severe pain
contraindications: Altered mental status
Acute intoxication or drug use
Pregnancy, except during delivery
Blunt or penetrating chest trauma, or pneumothorax
Craniofacial injury, traumatic brain injury, or raised intracranial pressure
Undifferentiated abdominal pain
Diving emergencies — decompression illness
Respiratory distress
Maxillofacial abnormality, facial trauma or burns
Status post retinal surgery
pearls: N2O diffuses out of blood INTO closed gas spaces — bowel, middle ear, pneumothorax — and expands them. That single property explains most of the contraindication list

Self-administered by the patient, so the patient must be able to understand and follow directions. The patient holds the mask, not the clinician — if they get too sedated the mask falls away, which is the built-in safety
Delivered as a 50/50 blend with oxygen in EMS, so it is never a hypoxic mixture
Among the few medications the national Scope of Practice Model names outright, at AEMT and Paramedic
